title: Imtiaz Ali's Main Vaapas Aaunga Is Officially IMDb's Most Anticipated Indian Film of 2026
excerpt: A Partition-era love story starring Diljit Dosanjh, Vedang Raina, Sharvari, and Naseeruddin Shah has outranked every blockbuster franchise on IMDb's annual poll.
body:
In a year that has given us spy sequels crossing ₹500 crore, mythological epics blocking 18-month schedules, and enough franchise films to fill an entire multiplex, the most anticipated Indian film of 2026 is none of those things.

It's a mid-budget romantic musical about the Partition.

IMDb's annual survey has crowned Imtiaz Ali's *Main Vaapas Aaunga* as the most anticipated Indian film and show of 2026, beating out Yash's *Toxic*, Ranbir Kapoor's *Ramayana*, Shah Rukh Khan's *King*, and every other tentpole that has dominated industry conversations this year.

## A Return to What Made Imtiaz Ali Matter

The filmmaker behind *Jab We Met*, *Rockstar*, and *Tamasha* has always been at his best when he tells stories about people searching for something they can't name. *Main Vaapas Aaunga* appears to be his most ambitious attempt yet — a love story set against the backdrop of the 1947 Partition, spanning generations and languages.

The cast is deliberate. Vedang Raina, who broke out in *The Archies*, takes the lead alongside Sharvari, fresh off her *Alpha* success. Diljit Dosanjh brings global star power (his North American arena tours have made him the most recognized Punjabi artist in the West). And Naseeruddin Shah anchors the emotional weight, as he has done for five decades of Indian cinema.

A.R. Rahman is composing the music. If that sentence alone doesn't tell you why people are excited, you may not have listened to the *Rockstar* or *Highway* soundtracks recently.

## Why a Partition Film Resonates With the Diaspora

Partition stories hold a specific gravity for NRI audiences. Most Indian families in the US, UK, and Canada carry some version of a Partition narrative — a grandparent's village that no longer exists on their side of the border, a family photograph that stops making sense after 1947, a language that moved with a train.

Imtiaz Ali's decision to tell a Partition story through music and romance rather than through violence and politics is a creative bet that could pay off enormously with diaspora audiences. The genre has seen literary successes (*The Shadow of the Sun*, Salman Rushdie's body of work) and cinematic attempts (*Gadar*, *Viceroy's House*), but a romantic musical in the Imtiaz Ali style — emotional, wandering, backed by Rahman — would be new territory.

## The Economics Tell a Story Too

*Main Vaapas Aaunga* is backed by Applause Entertainment and Window Seat Films. It doesn't have the ₹300+ crore budget of a *Ramayana* or the franchise safety net of a *Welcome to the Jungle*. Its June 12 release date puts it in direct competition with Akshay Kumar's *Bhooth Bangla* arriving on Netflix the same day and Bobby Deol's *Bandar* still running in theatres.

That a mid-budget, director-driven film with no established franchise has generated more anticipation than every blockbuster surrounding it says something about what audiences actually want in 2026. The trailer, which dropped recently, received an overwhelming response across social media. The film's songs are already dominating playlists before the movie has opened.

## What to Expect

The film releases in theatres on June 12, 2026. Music by A.R. Rahman is available through TIPS. If Imtiaz Ali delivers even a fraction of what *Rockstar* meant to a generation of young Indians who watched it in college hostels and PG accommodations across the country, this could be the film that defines the summer.

For the diaspora, it's simpler: this is a film about going back. The title says it. *Main Vaapas Aaunga* — I will come back. Every NRI has said that sentence at an airport at least once.

*Main Vaapas Aaunga releases in theatres on June 12, 2026. Produced by Applause Entertainment and Window Seat Films.*
author: Diaspora Desk
